title: Higher Cortical Functions: Aphasia and Lobar Syndromes

steps.tx: Acquired impairment of language processing caused by focal cerebral cortical damage in the dominant hemisphere (left hemisphere in over ninety-five percent of individuals) is designated as aphasia. Evaluating spontaneous fluency, auditory comprehension, and sentence repetition systematically categorises all classic clinical **aphasia types** and points directly to distinct neurovascular territories.

steps.tx: A non-fluent, expressive language disorder caused by infarction of the inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) within the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery is **Broca aphasia**. Patients exhibit halting, agrammatic, telegraphic speech produced with intense effort. Comprehension of spoken and written language is largely preserved, but repetition is markedly impaired.
steps.say: A non-fluent expressive language disorder caused by infarction of the inferior frontal gyrus within the superior division of the left middle cerebral artery is Broca aphasia. Patients exhibit halting, telegraphic speech produced with intense effort. Auditory comprehension is largely preserved, but sentence repetition is impaired.

steps.tx: In contrast, a fluent, receptive language disorder caused by ischaemic destruction of the posterior third of the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) in the inferior division of the left MCA is **Wernicke aphasia**. Speech is effortless, rapid, and melodic but completely devoid of meaning, contaminated by neologisms and phonemic paraphasias. Patients exhibit profound loss of comprehension and lack insight into their deficit.
steps.say: In contrast, a fluent receptive language disorder caused by ischemic destruction of the posterior superior temporal gyrus is Wernicke aphasia. Speech is effortless, rapid, and fluent but completely devoid of meaning, filled with neologisms. Patients exhibit profound loss of comprehension and lack insight into their deficit.

steps.tx: Direct bidirectional connection between Wernicke and Broca language areas is mediated by a prominent subcortical white matter association tract known as the **arcuate fasciculus**. Lesions interrupting this subcortical perisylvian bridge produce a distinctive disconnection syndrome, leaving cortical speech production and sensory decoding centres intact while destroying their intercommunication.

steps.tx: Interruption of the arcuate fasciculus or supramarginal gyrus produces the classical disconnection syndrome termed **conduction aphasia**. Characterised by fluent spontaneous speech and completely intact auditory comprehension, patients exhibit a disproportionate and severe inability to repeat spoken sentences, accompanied by frequent phonemic paraphasic errors during naming attempts.
steps.say: Interruption of the arcuate fasciculus produces the classical disconnection syndrome termed conduction aphasia. Characterized by fluent spontaneous speech and completely intact auditory comprehension, patients exhibit a disproportionate inability to repeat spoken sentences.

steps.tx: Massive infarction spanning both anterior and posterior branches of the dominant middle cerebral artery causes devastating **global aphasia**. Both expressive fluency and receptive comprehension are completely lost, rendering the patient mute or capable only of repeating stereotyped nonsense syllables. It is almost invariably accompanied by severe contralateral dense spastic hemiplegia and homonymous hemianopia.
steps.say: Massive infarction spanning both anterior and posterior branches of the dominant middle cerebral artery causes devastating global aphasia. Both expressive fluency and receptive comprehension are completely lost, rendering the patient mute. It is accompanied by severe contralateral spastic hemiplegia and hemianopia.

steps.tx: Cortical injury outside the language core produces distinct focal cognitive deficits. Infarction of the inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus) of the dominant hemisphere produces the classic tetrad of **Gerstmann syndrome**: agraphia (inability to write), acalculia (inability to perform mathematical operations), finger agnosia (inability to name or distinguish fingers), and right-left disorientation.

steps.tx: Conversely, acute injury to the non-dominant (right) parietal lobe produces the profound spatial neglect syndrome termed **hemispatial neglect** (anosognosia). Patients fail to respond to sensory stimuli or visual targets in the contralateral (left) hemispace, ignore the left side of their own body, and are completely unaware of severe left hemiplegia or neurological illness.
steps.say: Conversely, acute injury to the non-dominant right parietal lobe produces the profound spatial neglect syndrome termed hemispatial neglect. Patients fail to respond to stimuli in the contralateral left hemispace, ignore the left side of their body, and are completely unaware of left-sided paralysis.
